opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a great question, because people tend to lump all of these tasks together as "picking things up," but they're actually very different problems.

A package in a warehouse is, in some sense, a more structured problem. The environment is somewhat controlled: you've got bins, conveyor belts, consistent lighting, and a limited set of goals. You want to take the item out of the bin and put it in a box or a shipping container. You don't have to worry about a child running by or someone's grandmother's china. And the economic incentive is enormous, so companies have invested heavily in engineering that environment to make it friendlier to robots.

A dinner table is almost the opposite. Think about clearing a table after a meal: you've got glasses, some half full, plates with food on them, silverware that's thin and shiny and hard to see, napkins that are deformable, and everything is cluttered and overlapping. Every table is different and every home is different. And the cost of failure is higher, because if you drop a wine glass it shatters. So the variability and the stakes are much higher.

But even with packages, it's surprisingly hard, and that's what people don't appreciate. The packages themselves are incredibly diverse. You might have a rigid box, then a floppy polybag with clothing in it, then something in shrink wrap that's reflective and confuses the cameras, then a blister pack, then something transparent. Items are jumbled together in a bin, so they're partially occluded. The robot can't perfectly perceive where things are, it doesn't know the exact mass or center of mass, and it doesn't know the friction of the surface. Those small uncertainties in perception, in control, and in physics add up, and they're the reason grasping remains an open problem.

Humans do this effortlessly. A child can reach into a bin and grab anything. We take that for granted, but it reflects millions of years of evolution and a lifetime of practice. For robots, getting from, say, 95% reliability to 99.9% is where all the hard work is, and in a warehouse handling millions of items a day, that difference really matters.

So I'd say packages are a tractable stepping stone. They're hard enough to be a real research challenge, but structured enough that we're actually making progress and seeing deployments, whereas the dinner table is still a ways off.

r001.rationale: The response describes packages as varied, including reflective and transparent examples, but does not say their opacity makes them more manageable than dinner-table objects.

r002.rationale: It does not identify packages’ flat surfaces as making them easier to grasp.

r003.rationale: It says packages are jumbled together in a bin and partially occluded, making perception and grasping difficult.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss suction-based picking or finding a cup placement that avoids collisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing about packages is that they're a constrained version of the problem. If you walk into a warehouse, you're looking at objects that are mostly boxes, mostly rigid, mostly sitting on a conveyor belt or in a bin, and they're not changing much. Nobody's moving them around. There's no wine glass half full of liquid, no fork balanced on the edge of a plate, no kid reaching across to grab the bread. So you've eliminated a huge amount of the variability that makes a dinner table so hard.

And that matters, because grasping is fundamentally a problem of uncertainty. When a robot reaches for something, it doesn't know exactly where the object is, it doesn't know exactly how its own gripper will contact the surface, it doesn't know the friction, the mass distribution, whether the thing will slip. Every one of those uncertainties compounds. In a warehouse, you've narrowed the range on most of those. The object is probably a box. It probably has flat faces. It's probably not going to deform or spill.

But "more manageable" is a long way from "easy." Even with packages, you've got millions of distinct items. Amazon has something like hundreds of millions of products in their catalog, and they're constantly changing, so you can't just build a model of each one. You get polybags that crumple, boxes that are wedged under other boxes, things that are shiny and confuse the depth sensors, items that are heavier on one end than the other. A human picker sees all that in an instant and adjusts. The robot has to deal with it from noisy sensor data and a gripper that's far less dexterous than a human hand.

So I think of it as the right problem to work on. It's hard enough to be interesting, and there's real economic pull behind it, but it's structured enough that you can make progress. The dinner table is more like the grand challenge. We'll get there, but I'd rather earn our way up to it than start with the thing that's maximally hard in every dimension at once.

r001.rationale: The response describes packages as mostly rigid boxes but does not identify their opacity as a reason they are easier to handle.

r002.rationale: It says packages are likely to have flat faces as part of why the warehouse task is more constrained and manageable.

r003.rationale: It mentions objects in bins and boxes wedged under other boxes, but does not explain that random bin arrangements make grasp planning difficult.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss suction-based picking, choosing cup placement, or avoiding collisions with surrounding objects.

astra-6.text:
Well, packages are a more constrained problem. On a dinner table, you might have glasses, silverware, plates, bits of food—objects with very different properties, some fragile, some tangled together. With packages, you have a narrower range of things to deal with, and you can often use suction to pick them up.

But that doesn’t make it easy. A package might be a cardboard box, or it might be a plastic bag with something loose inside. It can deform when you touch it. The surface might be wrinkled, so you don’t get a good suction seal. And you don’t necessarily know where the weight is distributed. So even if you can see the package, figuring out where to grasp it and whether that grasp will hold is still a difficult problem.

r001.rationale: The response cites a narrower range of package types and suction as advantages, but does not identify opacity as a reason.

r002.rationale: It mentions wrinkled surfaces and difficulty getting a suction seal, but does not say packages’ flat surfaces make grasping easier.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about package shape and weight, but not random package arrangements in a bin as a source of grasp-planning difficulty.

r004.rationale: It mentions suction seals, but does not explain that bin picking requires placing the suction cup to avoid collisions with surrounding objects.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, packages are more constrained. At a dinner table, you might have glasses, silverware, plates, bits of food — objects with very different shapes and materials, all mixed together. With packages, you have a narrower range of things to deal with, and you can design the environment around the robot.

But that doesn’t mean grasping them is easy. A package might be a cardboard box, or it might be a floppy plastic bag with something inside. You don’t necessarily know its weight, where its centre of mass is, or what will happen when you pick it up. And if packages are piled together, you may only see part of each one. So even in this relatively structured setting, the robot has to make a decision with incomplete information: where can I get a reliable grasp, and how confident am I that it will hold?

r001.rationale: It says packages offer a narrower range and allow a robot-designed environment, but does not identify their opacity as a reason they are more manageable.

r002.rationale: It does not mention flat surfaces or connect them to easier grasping.

r003.rationale: It mentions packages piled together and partial visibility, but does not explain that random arrangements in a bin make grasp planning difficult.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss suction-based picking, suction-cup placement, or avoiding collisions with surrounding objects.
